description: A story about the most carefully chosen words on Earth -- the precise, deliberately ambiguous language of diplomacy, where 'frank exchange of views' means people argued fiercely.

content.content:
## The Language of Diplomacy

There is a kind of English where every single word is weighed, measured, and chosen with extreme care -- the English of international relations, the United Nations, and dealings between nations. **Diplomatic English** is a specialised register marked by extreme precision, deliberate ambiguity, and the strategic use of euphemism.

What makes it so unusual? Every word in a diplomatic statement is carefully chosen. Ambiguity is often *intentional*, allowing parties to "save face." Understatement is preferred over direct confrontation. And the language must be translatable and culturally neutral, since it will be read in dozens of languages. In this chapter we will learn how language functions in diplomatic contexts, how to recognise and decode euphemism in political speech, how international organisations use English, and how word choice shapes the way the whole world understands global events. By the end, you will be able to read between the lines of a UN press statement.

## UN Language and the Art of Euphemism

The **United Nations** uses six official languages -- Arabic, Chinese, English, French, Russian, and Spanish -- but English is the primary working language for most UN business. A core vocabulary recurs across diplomacy: a **resolution** is a formal decision by the General Assembly or Security Council; **sovereignty** is a state's right to govern itself without outside interference; **multilateral** involves three or more parties and **bilateral** two; **sanctions** are measures imposed to pressure a state; **ratification** is formal approval of a treaty; a **preamble** is the introductory statement of a treaty; **non-binding** means advisory rather than legally obligatory; and the **veto** is the power of the five permanent Security Council members to block any substantive resolution.

But the real art lies in **diplomatic speech acts**, where polite phrases carry hidden meanings. "We note with concern..." means "we disapprove strongly." "Constructive dialogue" means significant disagreement exists. "We reserve our position" means "we will not commit to this." "A frank and candid exchange" means a heated argument. "The matter is under review" means no decision will come soon. And "We urge all parties to exercise restraint" means someone is about to do something dangerous.

Consider decoding an actual-style statement: "The Security Council held a frank and comprehensive exchange of views on the deteriorating situation... Members expressed deep concern... and urged all parties to exercise maximum restraint." Decoded, this reads: the members argued fiercely and could not agree ("frank exchange"); things are getting significantly worse ("deteriorating"); there is strong disapproval ("deep concern"); and at least one side is using or threatening violence ("urged restraint"). The crucial skill is understanding **graduated intensity** -- the scale runs from "noted" (weakest) through "concerned," "deeply concerned," "gravely concerned," all the way to "condemned" (strongest). Reading these gradations accurately is essential for interpreting international news.

questions.task: In diplomatic English, what does 'a frank and candid exchange of views' usually mean?

options.text: A heated argument where the parties could not agree

questions.solution: Diplomatic euphemism turns conflict into polite language. 'Frank and candid exchange' signals a heated argument and significant disagreement.

questions.task: What is the 'veto' in the UN Security Council?

options.text: The power of the five permanent members to block any substantive resolution
The opening statement of a resolution

questions.solution: The veto is the power held by the five permanent Security Council members (the P5) to block any substantive resolution, regardless of how others vote.

questions.task: Why is 'graduated intensity' important in diplomatic language?

options.text: It measures how loudly diplomats speak
It counts the number of countries present
It signals how strong a position is, from 'noted' (weak) to 'condemned' (strong)
It refers to the brightness of the room

questions.solution: Diplomatic language uses a scale of intensity -- noted, concerned, deeply concerned, gravely concerned, condemned -- and reading these gradations correctly is essential for interpreting statements.

questions.task: What does 'sovereignty' mean in diplomatic vocabulary?

options.text: The power to veto a resolution
A state's right to govern itself without external interference

questions.solution: Sovereignty is a state's right to self-governance without outside interference. Reaffirming commitment to a country's sovereignty often signals a threat to its borders or independence.

## International Organisations and National Styles

English plays a central role across the world's major international organisations, each of which has developed its own specialised vocabulary. The **United Nations** (founded 1945, 193 members) uses extremely precise legal English in its resolutions. The **European Union** has 24 official languages, but English remains the most-used working language even after Brexit, complete with its own "Eurojargon" ("subsidiarity," "acquis communautaire"). **NATO** uses English and French, with military terminology like "rules of engagement" and "theatre of operations." The **World Health Organization** applies diplomatic language to health ("public health emergency of international concern"), and the **World Trade Organization** has its own trade vocabulary ("tariff," "dumping," "most-favoured-nation status"). Effective international communication requires familiarity not just with general English but with the specific register of the relevant institution.

Fascinatingly, different countries have distinct diplomatic styles *even when all are using English*. **British diplomacy** is known for understatement and indirectness -- "I hear what you say" often means "I disagree and won't discuss it further," and "with the greatest respect" frequently precedes a sharp disagreement. **American diplomacy** is more direct, using phrases like "Let me be clear..." to signal firm positions. **Norwegian diplomacy** is famous for its peace-facilitation role and emphasises inclusivity and consensus: "We believe all parties should have a seat at the table." **Chinese diplomacy** is highly structured and formal, with phrases like "hurt the feelings of the Chinese people" carrying specific political weight. You can see the contrast in how each expresses displeasure: the British say "We are somewhat disappointed by the lack of progress"; the Americans say "Let me be frank: this is unacceptable"; the Norwegians say "We encourage all parties to renew their commitment"; and the Chinese say "This action seriously undermines mutual trust." Underneath it all, **euphemism** serves vital functions: it lets parties express displeasure without provoking confrontation, enables face-saving, and keeps channels of communication open.

questions.solution: Despite the UK leaving, English remains the most-used working language of the EU, complete with its own 'Eurojargon' such as 'subsidiarity'.

questions.task: British diplomacy is especially known for which feature?

options.text: Understatement and indirectness, where 'I hear what you say' can mean 'I disagree'
Always saying exactly what is meant

questions.solution: British diplomatic style favours understatement and indirectness. 'I hear what you say' often means 'I disagree and do not wish to discuss it further.'

questions.task: What important function does euphemism serve in diplomacy?

options.text: It makes statements longer for no reason
It lets parties express displeasure without provoking confrontation and enables face-saving
It hides the meaning from the speaker's own side

questions.solution: Euphemism allows diplomats to express disapproval without direct confrontation, enables face-saving, and keeps communication channels open.

questions.task: Norwegian diplomacy is particularly associated with:

options.text: A peace-facilitation role emphasising inclusivity and consensus

questions.solution: Norway is known for its 'peace diplomacy' and facilitation role, with language emphasising inclusivity, dialogue, and consensus -- 'all parties should have a seat at the table.'

## Summary

**Diplomatic English** is a specialised register defined by precision, strategic ambiguity, euphemism, and graduated levels of intensity. The **United Nations** and other international organisations -- the EU, NATO, WHO, WTO -- have each developed specific vocabularies and conventions, so interpreting global news requires familiarity with their registers. **Euphemism** serves crucial functions: it allows parties to express displeasure without confrontation, enables face-saving, and keeps communication open. Reading **graduated intensity** -- from "noted" to "condemned" -- is essential for understanding what statements really mean. And remarkably, different **national diplomatic styles** persist even when everyone speaks English, from British understatement to American directness to Norwegian consensus-building, reflecting deeper cultural values about directness, hierarchy, and conflict.
